title: What Does Islam Really Say About Jesus?
summary: The genuinely high, honoured status Jesus holds in Islamic teaching — surprising to many non-Muslims — and exactly where Islamic and Christian belief about him actually diverge.

body.text: A surprise for many Christian family members specifically

If you come from a Christian background, family members may assume becoming Muslim means rejecting or disrespecting Jesus entirely. In fact, Jesus (Isa, in Arabic) holds a position of major honour in Islamic teaching — genuinely surprising to many people encountering this for the first time.
Jesus as one of the most important prophets

Jesus is named in the Quran more times than the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) himself, and is counted among the small group of "Ul-ul-Azm" (Prophets of Strong Will) — the most significant prophets in Islamic teaching, alongside Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Muhammad. An entire chapter of the Quran (Surah Maryam) is named after his mother.

body.translation: She said, "How can I have a boy while no man has touched me?" [The angel] said, "Thus [it will be]; Allah creates what He wills."

body.text: The virgin birth of Jesus, through Mary, is directly affirmed in the Quran — a point of genuine shared ground with Christian belief that surprises many people on both sides of this conversation.

Mary (Maryam) is described in the Quran as chosen and purified above all women of her time, and is the only woman named directly in the Quran's text. Her honoured status in Islamic teaching is, if anything, comparably strong to her status in Christian tradition.

Being honest about the real difference matters as much as the common ground: Islamic teaching holds that Jesus was a human prophet and messenger, not divine and not God incarnate, and does not accept the crucifixion-and-resurrection narrative in the form Christian theology holds it (Islamic teaching describes Jesus as raised to God rather than killed on the cross, with scholarly discussion on the exact details). Islamic teaching also affirms Jesus will return before the end of times, a point of some genuine overlap with certain Christian eschatological beliefs, though understood differently in its specifics.

body.question: So do Muslims believe Jesus performed miracles?
body.answer: Yes — the Quran describes Jesus healing the blind and those with leprosy, and reviving the dead, by God's permission specifically (a point Islamic teaching emphasises: the miracles are attributed to God acting through him, not evidence of his own divinity).

body.question: What's a good way to explain this to a Christian family member worried I now "reject" Jesus?
body.answer: It can help to lead with the genuine common ground first — the virgin birth, his status as a major prophet, the honour given to Mary — before explaining the specific, real difference about his divinity, since starting from what's actually shared tends to be received far better than starting from the disagreement.

body.question: Did the extent of Jesus's and Mary's honoured status in Islamic teaching surprise you? How might this change a conversation with Christian family or friends?
